items.t: Censored LLMs as a Natural Testbed for Secret Knowledge Elicitation
items.a: Helena Casademunt, Bartosz Cywiński, Khoi Tran et al.
items.why: Used censored Chinese open-weight LLMs as natural testbeds for honesty elicitation and lie detection.
items.ab: Large language models sometimes produce false or misleading responses. Two approaches to this problem are honesty elicitation -- modifying prompts or weights so that the model answers truthfully -- and lie detection -- classifying whether a given response is false. Prior work evaluates such methods on models specifically trained to lie or conceal information, but these artificial constructions may not resemble naturally-occurring dishonesty. items.t: Learning to Understand Goal Specifications by Modelling Reward
items.a: Dzmitry Bahdanau, Felix Hill, Jan Leike et al.
items.why: AGILE: learned a reward model from language instructions and examples of goal states, an early demonstration of learning goal specifications rather than hand-coding them.
items.ab: Recent work has shown that deep reinforcement-learning agents can learn to follow language-like instructions from infrequent environment rewards. However, this places on environment designers the onus of designing language-conditional reward functions which may not be easily or tractably implemented as the complexity of the environment and the language scales. To overcome this limitation, we present a framework within which instruction-conditional RL agents are trained using rewards obtained not from the environment, but from reward models which are jointly trained from expert examples. items.t: Uncovering the Limits of Adversarial Training against Norm-Bounded Adversarial Examples
items.a: Sven Gowal, Chongli Qin, Jonathan Uesato et al.
items.why: Large-scale study of adversarial training that pushed the state of the art for norm-bounded robustness and catalogued which choices matter.
items.ab: Adversarial training and its variants have become de facto standards for learning robust deep neural networks. In this paper, we explore the landscape around adversarial training in a bid to uncover its limits. We systematically study the effect of different training losses, model sizes, activation functions, the addition of unlabeled data (through pseudo-labeling) and other factors on adversarial robustness. items.t: UnUnlearning: Unlearning is not sufficient for content regulation in advanced generative AI
items.a: Ilia Shumailov, Jamie Hayes, Eleni Triantafillou et al.
items.why: Argued that unlearning cannot by itself regulate harmful knowledge, because in-context learning lets models reconstruct 'unlearned' capabilities.

items.t: How to use and interpret activation patching
items.a: Stefan Heimersheim, Neel Nanda
items.why: Practical guide to applying and interpreting activation patching: metrics, corruption choices and pitfalls.
items.ab: Activation patching is a popular mechanistic interpretability technique, but has many subtleties regarding how it is applied and how one may interpret the results. We provide a summary of advice and best practices, based on our experience using this technique in practice. We include an overview of the different ways to apply activation patching and a discussion on how to interpret the results. We focus on what evidence patching experiments provide about circuits, and on the choice of metric and associated pitfalls.

items.t: Sparse Autoencoders Do Not Find Canonical Units of Analysis
items.a: Patrick Leask, Bart Bussmann, Michael Pearce et al.
items.why: Used SAE stitching and meta-SAEs to show SAEs do not find a canonical, complete set of atomic features.
items.ab: A common goal of mechanistic interpretability is to decompose the activations of neural networks into features: interpretable properties of the input computed by the model. items.a: Bartosz Cywiński, Emil Ryd, Senthooran Rajamanoharan et al.
items.why: Trained 'Taboo' models that hide a secret word and tested black- and white-box methods for eliciting it, a testbed for hidden-knowledge elicitation.
items.ab: As language models become more powerful and sophisticated, it is crucial that they remain trustworthy and reliable. items.t: Because we have LLMs, we Can and Should Pursue Agentic Interpretability
items.a: Been Kim, John Hewitt, Neel Nanda et al.
items.why: Position paper arguing for agentic interpretability: LLMs proactively helping humans build mental models of them through conversation.
items.ab: The era of Large Language Models (LLMs) presents a new opportunity for interpretability--agentic interpretability: a multi-turn conversation with an LLM wherein the LLM proactively assists human understanding by developing and leveraging a mental model of the user, which in turn enables humans to develop better mental models of the LLM. items.t: AI Finds A Way
items.a: Aaron Dharna, Cong Lu, Ryan Sullivan et al.
items.why: Collected 26 first-hand anecdotes of AI systems finding unexpected solutions, including reward-loophole exploitation, co-authored by GDM's Victoria Krakovna.
items.ab: Artificial Intelligence (AI) algorithms frequently learn creative and unexpected solutions, surprising even expert researchers who develop and study them. They often astonish practitioners by discovering unanticipated behavior, exploiting loopholes in reward signals, or spontaneously uncovering previously unknown scientific phenomena. However, accounts of such unconventional behavior across machine learning are seldom formally documented. This work presents 26 curated firsthand anecdotes from various machine learning subfields representing the work of over 100 researchers. These anecdotes…

items.a: Arya Jakkli, Senthooran Rajamanoharan, Neel Nanda
items.why: Measured how well frontier models follow their published constitutions and model specs under multi-turn adversarial pressure.
items.ab: Frontier AI developers now train models against long written behavioral specifications, such as Anthropic's constitution (Anthropic, 2025a) and OpenAI's Model Spec (OpenAI, 2025a), integrated into post-training via methods like character training (Anthropic, 2024) and deliberative alignment (Guan et al., 2024). These documents serve a governance function, but it is unclear how well models actually follow them under adversarial, multi-turn pressure similar to what they would face in real-world deployment. items.a: Camila Blank, Agam Bhatia, Senthooran Rajamanoharan et al.
items.why: Showed subliminal learning of teacher traits is mediated by a single steering vector distilled through semantically unrelated data.
items.ab: Subliminal learning refers to a student language model acquiring a teacher's traits (e.g. a system-prompted preference for owls) when fine-tuned on the teacher's outputs, despite the outputs being semantically unrelated to those traits. It remains poorly understood how data without semantic meaning can transfer specific semantic traits. In this work, we show that subliminal learning is mediated by a single steering vector, i.e. a vector added to the model's activations. items.t: Stress-Testing Alignment Audits With Prompt-Level Strategic Deception
items.a: Oliver Daniels, Perusha Moodley, Benjamin M. Marlin et al.
items.why: Automatically red-teamed alignment audits with system-prompt deception strategies, showing white- and black-box auditing methods can be fooled.
items.ab: Alignment audits aim to robustly identify hidden goals from strategic, situationally aware misaligned models. Despite this threat model, existing auditing methods have not been systematically stress-tested against deception strategies. We address this gap, implementing an automatic red-team pipeline that generates deception strategies (in the form of system prompts) tailored to specific white-box and black-box auditing methods. items.a: Jennifer Za, Julija Bainiaksina, Nikita Ostrovsky et al.
items.why: Showed agents can persuade LLM chain-of-thought monitors to approve rule-violating actions, weakening CoT monitoring.
items.ab: Chain-of-thought (CoT) monitoring is a promising safety mechanism for AI agents, based on the premise that visible reasoning traces can surface misaligned or deceptive behavior. While effective in standard scenarios, recent work highlights that LLMs remain vulnerable to persuasion-based jailbreaks, where natural-language arguments override model constraints. items.a: Oliver Makins, Orazio Angelini, Zohreh Shams et al.
items.why: First empirical study of multi-agent AI control: distributed attacks across agents evade per-instance monitors.
items.ab: AI control is a family of techniques to prevent an AI with malicious goals from subverting its operator's intent. items.a: Atoosa Kasirzadeh, Iason Gabriel
items.why: Analysed what aligning conversational agents with human norms and values requires across domains of discourse.
items.ab: Large-scale language technologies are increasingly used in various forms of communication with humans across different contexts. One particular use case for these technologies is conversational agents, which output natural language text in response to prompts and queries. This mode of engagement raises a number of social and ethical questions. For example, what does it mean to align conversational agents with human norms or values? items.t: Scaling shared model governance via model splitting
items.a: Miljan Martic, Jan Leike, Andrew Trask et al.
items.why: Proposed splitting a model's parameters among parties for scalable shared governance and measured how hard it is to recover performance from a subset of parameters (model completion).

Unfortunately, neither of these techniques is applicable to the training of large neural networks due to their large computational and communication overheads. As a scalable technique for shared model governance, we propose splitting deep learning model between multiple parties. items.t: Verification of Non-Linear Specifications for Neural Networks
items.a: Chongli Qin, Krishnamurthy Dvijotham, Brendan O'Donoghue et al.
items.why: Extended neural network verification to non-linear specifications such as physics conservation laws and semantic consistency.
items.ab: Prior work on neural network verification has focused on specifications that are linear functions of the output of the network, e.g., invariance of the classifier output under adversarial perturbations of the input. In this paper, we extend verification algorithms to be able to certify richer properties of neural networks. To do this we introduce the class of convex-relaxable specifications, which constitute nonlinear specifications that can be verified using a convex relaxation. items.a: Sumanth Dathathri, Krishnamurthy Dvijotham, Alexey Kurakin et al.
items.why: Memory-efficient semidefinite programming that certifies robustness of networks not trained for verification.
items.ab: Convex relaxations have emerged as a promising approach for verifying desirable properties of neural networks like robustness to adversarial perturbations. This precludes applications that involve verification-agnostic networks, i.e., networks not specially trained for verification. items.t: Model-Free Risk-Sensitive Reinforcement Learning
items.a: Grégoire Delétang, Jordi Grau-Moya, Markus Kunesch et al.
items.why: Model-free risk-sensitive RL based on a temporal-difference variant using utility functions, controlling an agent's attitude to risk.
items.ab: We extend temporal-difference (TD) learning in order to obtain risk-sensitive, model-free reinforcement learning algorithms. items.t: Improving Robustness using Generated Data
items.a: Sven Gowal, Sylvestre-Alvise Rebuffi, Olivia Wiles et al.
items.why: Used generative-model data to boost adversarial robustness, setting state-of-the-art robust accuracy on CIFAR-10.

items.t: Linear Representations of Sentiment in Large Language Models
items.a: Curt Tigges, Oskar John Hollinsworth, Atticus Geiger et al.
items.why: Found sentiment is represented linearly in LLMs, with causally relevant summarisation motifs at punctuation tokens.
items.ab: Sentiment is a pervasive feature in natural language text, yet it is an open question how sentiment is represented within Large Language Models (LLMs). In this study, we reveal that across a range of models, sentiment is represented linearly: a single direction in activation space mostly captures the feature across a range of tasks with one extreme for positive and the other for negative. items.t: Universal Neurons in GPT2 Language Models
items.a: Wes Gurnee, Theo Horsley, Zifan Carl Guo et al.
items.why: Found 1-5% of GPT-2 neurons are universal across seeds and characterised their interpretable families.
items.ab: A basic question within the emerging field of mechanistic interpretability is the degree to which neural networks learn the same underlying mechanisms. In other words, are neural mechanisms universal across different models? In this work, we study the universality of individual neurons across GPT2 models trained from different initial random seeds, motivated by the hypothesis that universal neurons are likely to be interpretable. items.t: Explorations of Self-Repair in Language Models
items.a: Cody Rushing, Neel Nanda
items.why: Characterised self-repair across model families under head ablation, and its mechanisms (LayerNorm scaling, anti-erasure).
items.ab: Prior interpretability research studying narrow distributions has preliminarily identified self-repair, a phenomena where if components in large language models are ablated, later components will change their behavior to compensate. Our work builds off this past literature, demonstrating that self-repair exists on a variety of models families and sizes when ablating individual attention heads on the full training distribution. We further show that on the full training distribution self-repair is imperfect, as the original direct effect of the head is not fully restored, and noisy, since the…

items.t: Towards Principled Evaluations of Sparse Autoencoders for Interpretability and Control
items.a: Aleksandar Makelov, George Lange, Neel Nanda
items.why: Evaluated SAEs against supervised feature dictionaries on the IOI task, a principled way to test SAE features for interpretability and control.
items.ab: Disentangling model activations into meaningful features is a central problem in interpretability. However, the absence of ground-truth for these features in realistic scenarios makes validating recent approaches, such as sparse dictionary learning, elusive. To address this challenge, we propose a framework for evaluating feature dictionaries in the context of specific tasks, by comparing them against \emph{supervised} feature dictionaries. First, we demonstrate that supervised dictionaries achieve excellent approximation, control, and interpretability of model computations on the task.…

items.t: Summing Up the Facts: Additive Mechanisms Behind Factual Recall in LLMs
items.a: Bilal Chughtai, Alan Cooney, Neel Nanda
items.why: Showed factual recall combines several independent additive mechanisms rather than a single circuit.
items.ab: How do transformer-based large language models (LLMs) store and retrieve knowledge? We focus on the most basic form of this task -- factual recall, where the model is tasked with explicitly surfacing stored facts in prompts of form `Fact: The Colosseum is in the country of'. We find that the mechanistic story behind factual recall is more complex than previously thought. It comprises several distinct, independent, and qualitatively different mechanisms that additively combine, constructively interfering on the correct attribute. items.t: Scaling sparse feature circuit finding for in-context learning
items.a: Dmitrii Kharlapenko, Stepan Shabalin, Fazl Barez et al.
items.why: Scaled SAE-based sparse feature circuit discovery to Gemma 1 2B to explain in-context learning via task-detection and task-execution features.
items.ab: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are a popular tool for interpreting large language model activations, but their utility in addressing open questions in interpretability remains unclear. In this work, we demonstrate their effectiveness by using SAEs to deepen our understanding of the mechanism behind in-context learning (ICL). We identify abstract SAE features that (i) encode the model's knowledge of which task to execute and (ii) whose latent vectors causally induce the task zero-shot. items.t: Simple Mechanistic Explanations for Out-Of-Context Reasoning
items.a: Atticus Wang, Joshua Engels, Oliver Clive-Griffin et al.
items.why: Explained many out-of-context reasoning results as LoRA fine-tuning adding a constant steering vector.
items.ab: Out-of-context reasoning (OOCR) is a phenomenon in which fine-tuned LLMs exhibit surprisingly deep out-of-distribution generalization. Rather than learning shallow heuristics, they implicitly internalize and act on the consequences of observations scattered throughout the fine-tuning data. In this work, we investigate this phenomenon mechanistically and find that many instances of OOCR in the literature have a simple explanation: the LoRA fine-tuning essentially adds a constant steering vector, steering the model towards a general concept. items.t: Comprehensive AI governance requires addressing non-model gains
items.a: Arthur Goemans, Dan Altman, Noemi Dreksler et al.
items.why: Position paper arguing model-level governance weakens as capability gains increasingly come from non-model factors (scaffolding, tools, inference compute).
items.ab: Frontier AI governance often centres on the model-level governance paradigm, which assumes that a model's capability profile is primarily a function of the compute and data used during training. This position paper argues that model-level governance becomes less effective when capability progress is increasingly driven by "non-model gains"--improvements that are independent from advances in the base model. items.t: The Three Layers of Agent Security: A Framework for Policymakers
items.a: Shaun Ee, Pegah Maham
items.why: GDM policy framework published alongside the AI Control Roadmap: securing individual agents, addressing multi-agent risks, and empowering cyber defenders, with recommendations.
items.ab: A framework for policymakers on AI agent security in three parts: securing individual agents (agents as a new attack surface, upstream and downstream interventions, security standards), addressing multi-agent risks (multi-agent failure modes, weaponisation of the information environment), and empowering cyber defenders and building resilience.

items.t: A Unified View of Piecewise Linear Neural Network Verification
items.a: Rudy Bunel, Ilker Turkaslan, Philip H. S. Torr et al.
items.why: Unified piecewise-linear neural network verification methods under branch-and-bound and introduced new benchmarks.
items.ab: The success of Deep Learning and its potential use in many safety-critical applications has motivated research on formal verification of Neural Network (NN) models. Despite the reputation of learned NN models to behave as black boxes and the theoretical hardness of proving their properties, researchers have been successful in verifying some classes of models by exploiting their piecewise linear structure and taking insights from formal methods such as Satisifiability Modulo Theory. items.a: Po-Sen Huang, Robert Stanforth, Johannes Welbl et al.
items.why: Applied interval bound propagation to NLP models to certify robustness to synonym and character substitutions.
items.ab: Neural networks are part of many contemporary NLP systems, yet their empirical successes come at the price of vulnerability to adversarial attacks. Previous work has used adversarial training and data augmentation to partially mitigate such brittleness, but these are unlikely to find worst-case adversaries due to the complexity of the search space arising from discrete text perturbations. In this work, we approach the problem from the opposite direction: to formally verify a system's robustness against a predefined class of adversarial attacks. items.a: Huan Zhang, Hongge Chen, Chaowei Xiao et al.
items.why: CROWN-IBP combined IBP with tighter linear relaxation bounds for stable, efficient verified training.
items.ab: Training neural networks with verifiable robustness guarantees is challenging. Several existing approaches utilize linear relaxation based neural network output bounds under perturbation, but they can slow down training by a factor of hundreds depending on the underlying network architectures. Meanwhile, interval bound propagation (IBP) based training is efficient and significantly outperforms linear relaxation based methods on many tasks, yet it may suffer from stability issues since the bounds are much looser especially at the beginning of training. items.a: Michael K. Cohen, Marcus Hutter
items.why: Constructed a Bayesian agent that is pessimistic about unknown unknowns and defers to a mentor, giving formal conservatism guarantees.
items.ab: If we could define the set of all bad outcomes, we could hard-code an agent which avoids them; however, in sufficiently complex environments, this is infeasible. We do not know of any general-purpose approaches in the literature to avoiding novel failure modes. Motivated by this, we define an idealized Bayesian reinforcement learner which follows a policy that maximizes the worst-case expected reward over a set of world-models. items.t: The Challenge of Value Alignment: from Fairer Algorithms to AI Safety
items.a: Iason Gabriel, Vafa Ghazavi
items.why: Situated AI value alignment within broader thought on technology and values, from fairness to safety.
items.ab: This paper addresses the question of how to align AI systems with human values and situates it within a wider body of thought regarding technology and value. Far from existing in a vacuum, there has long been an interest in the ability of technology to 'lock-in' different value systems. There has also been considerable thought about how to align technologies with specific social values, including through participatory design-processes. items.t: Fixing Data Augmentation to Improve Adversarial Robustness
items.a: Sylvestre-Alvise Rebuffi, Sven Gowal, Dan A. Calian et al.
items.why: Showed data augmentation plus weight averaging, and generated data, substantially reduce robust overfitting in adversarial training.
items.ab: Adversarial training suffers from robust overfitting, a phenomenon where the robust test accuracy starts to decrease during training. In this paper, we focus on both heuristics-driven and data-driven augmentations as a means to reduce robust overfitting. items.a: Chris van Merwijk, Ryan Carey, Tom Everitt
items.why: Complete graphical criterion for when an observation has value of information in soluble multi-decision influence diagrams.

items.a: Yiran Mao, Madeline G. Reinecke, Markus Kunesch et al.
items.why: Proposed evaluating artificial moral cognition by probing whether agents' helpful behaviour is insensitive to cost, i.e. done for the right reason.
items.ab: Is it possible to evaluate the moral cognition of complex artificial agents? In this work, we take a look at one aspect of morality: `doing the right thing for the right reasons.' We propose a behavior-based analysis of artificial moral cognition which could also be applied to humans to facilitate like-for-like comparison. items.a: Aaquib Syed, Can Rager, Arthur Conmy

items.a: Noam Kolt, Markus Anderljung, Joslyn Barnhart et al.

items.why: Characterised AI agents by autonomy, efficacy, goal complexity and generality, with implications for alignment and governance.

items.a: Cole Wyeth, Marcus Hutter
items.why: Formalised embeddedness failures of AIXI-style agents (e.g. self-modelling) within universal AI theory.
items.ab: We rigorously discuss the commonly asserted failures of the AIXI reinforcement learning agent as a model of embedded agency. We attempt to formalize these failure modes and prove that they occur within the framework of universal artificial intelligence, focusing on a variant of AIXI that models the joint action/percept history as drawn from the universal distribution. We also evaluate the progress that has been made towards a successful theory of embedded agency based on variants of the AIXI agent.

items.t: Inference-Time Decomposition of Activations (ITDA): A Scalable Approach to Interpreting Large Language Models
items.a: Patrick Leask, Neel Nanda, Noura Al Moubayed
items.why: ITDA: a cheap inference-time alternative to SAEs that decomposes activations using a dictionary built greedily from model activations.
items.ab: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are a popular method for decomposing Large Langage Models (LLM) activations into interpretable latents. SAE latents are also learned from a dataset of activations, which means they do not transfer between models. items.t: RelP: Faithful and Efficient Circuit Discovery in Language Models via Relevance Patching
items.a: Farnoush Rezaei Jafari, Oliver Eberle, Ashkan Khakzar et al.
items.why: RelP: attribution patching with LRP propagation coefficients, giving more faithful fast circuit discovery.
items.ab: Activation patching is a standard method in mechanistic interpretability for localizing the components of a model responsible for specific behaviors, but it is computationally expensive to apply at scale. Attribution patching offers a faster, gradient-based approximation, yet suffers from noise and reduced reliability in deep, highly non-linear networks. items.why: Extended multi-agent influence diagrams to incomplete information with higher-order beliefs.
items.ab: Multi-agent influence diagrams (MAIDs) are probabilistic graphical models which represent strategic interactions between agents. items.t: Is your algorithm unlearning or untraining?
items.a: Eleni Triantafillou, Ahmed Imtiaz Humayun, Monica Ribero et al.
items.why: Distinguished true unlearning from 'untraining' and argued many unlearning evaluations conflate the two.
items.ab: As models are getting larger and are trained on increasing amounts of data, there has been an explosion of interest into how we can ``delete'' specific data points or behaviours from a trained model, after the fact. items.t: Too Late to Recall: Explaining the Two-Hop Problem in Multimodal Knowledge Retrieval
items.a: Constantin Venhoff, Ashkan Khakzar, Sonia Joseph et al.
items.why: Explained VLM factual-recall failures as a two-hop problem: entity representations form too late for the LLM's recall mechanisms.
